Held-out accuracy

Prediction is not a recipe. These probabilities describe associations in one wine dataset. Changing an ingredient does not establish a causal improvement. Rare quality scores have very limited evidence.

The data behind the model

1,599 Portuguese red Vinho Verde wines, 11 laboratory measurements, and sensory quality scores from 3 to 8.

Original UCI dataset, not a sample of all wines. There are no grape, producer, vintage, or tasting-panel identifiers available for a stronger external validation.

Dataset and attribution ↗

How the evaluation works

  1. Keep repeated measurements together.
  2. Reserve one holdout.
  3. Learn inside each training fold.Fit bin boundaries, learn the network, and estimate probabilities afresh in each of five folds.
  4. Select before looking at the holdout.Mean validation macro-F1 selects the overall model and the network used in this explorer.
  5. Evaluate frozen models.All final holdout scores use identical rows. The interactive network remains fitted on training data only.

From the R project to this Python version

Preserved

The original red-wine dataset, six quality classes, Bayesian networks, AIC/BIC comparison, the original seven prior arrows as a separate experimental condition, and probabilistic inference.

Corrected

Split before learning; repeat preprocessing and structure learning inside validation; evaluate the correct AIC model; condition on all supplied evidence; include simple baselines and class-sensitive metrics.

Deliberately changed

Training-only quantile bins replace Hartemink. pyAgrum greedy hill climbing replaces the three R search methods. Networks have at most three parents per node; BDeu parameter smoothing uses equivalent sample size 5. This is a documented rebuild, not an exact numerical reproduction.

Still limited

No independent wine population, causal validation, or extra rare examples. No promise of higher accuracy. Bootstrap intervals quantify holdout sampling uncertainty, not every source of uncertainty. Structure-averaging and Hartemink parity remain future work.
